html:
An agency set up in 1881, run by European creditors, that took over a large part of the Ottoman Empire's tax income to pay back its foreign debts.

From the Crimean War on, the empire had borrowed heavily in London and Paris, often to pay interest on older loans. In 1875 it stopped paying. Under the Decree of Muharrem of 1881, issued by Abdul Hamid II, the debt was cut and an administration was formed to collect certain taxes directly: salt, tobacco, silk, stamps, spirits and fishing.

Its council had members for British, French, German, Austrian, Italian, Dutch and Ottoman creditors. It grew into a vast bureaucracy of its own, with thousands of staff, more than some ministries. It also backed foreign investment, such as guarantees for railway lines like the Baghdad Railway. It worked alongside the Imperial Ottoman Bank.

For Ottoman patriots and later Turkish nationalists it stood for lost sovereignty. After the empire fell, the debt was divided among its successor states under the Treaty of Lausanne of 1923, and the Turkish Republic finished paying its share in 1954.
sum: An agency set up in 1881, run by European creditors, that took over a large part of the Ottoman Empire's tax income to pay back its foreign debts.
